prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Troops in Jamaica captured an armed man Monday who had barged onto a Canadian airliner, robbed passengers and held six crew members hostage, Jamaica Information Minister Daryl Vaz said. A hostage-taker commandeered a CanJet flight at Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The crew members were not harmed, Vaz said. The hijacking suspect, described as a "mentally challenged" man in his 20s, had demanded that the Boeing 737 be flown to Cuba. The military captured him around 7 a.m. local time. The FBI helped Jamaican authorities handle the situation at the Jamaican government's request, a U.S. government source told CNN. The CanJet flight from Halifax, Canada, had made a scheduled landing at Sangster International Airport in the Jamaican resort city of Montego Bay and was scheduled to continue to Santa Clara, Cuba. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who was in Jamaica, told reporters that he planned to travel to Montego Bay to meet with Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding. Harper has been following the airplane security breach and may meet with the plane's crew later today. "The hijacking is that from a mentally challenged youngster and not anything that would be of concern in terms of an international incident," Vaz said. The suspect gained access to the plane Sunday night through the terminal in "a breach of security" that "will be investigated," Deputy Police Commissioner Owen Ellington told CNN. The gunman fired a shot in the boarding bridge as he entered, said CanJet Airlines Vice President Kent Woodside. No one was hit. CanJet Flight 918 was carrying 174 passengers and eight crew members, Woodside said. All the passengers were Canadian, he said. The suspect took an undisclosed number of passengers and crew members hostage before releasing all the passengers and two crew members, said Elizabeth Scotton, a spokeswoman for the company that manages the airport. Two of the six crew members who remained inside the plane Monday locked themselves in the cockpit, Vaz said. The suspect's father and Golding, who flew in by helicopter, were among those who negotiated with the gunman before his capture. The country's minister of national security also was at hand. The released passengers were taken to a hotel, and the airport was shut down for a time, Vaz said. The airport reopened shortly after the standoff, Woodside said. A CanJet airliner was on its way to Jamaica, he said, to take passengers on to Cuba or back to Canada. Christian Gosselin, a passenger on the flight, told his father that the gunman demanded cash from the plane's occupants. Vaz confirmed the account. "The guy wanted to have all their money," said Gosselin's father, Alphonse. "He [my son] told his girlfriend to take all the money and just take her passport and credit card and put it in her back pocket." Christian Gosselin was part of a 25-person wedding party headed to Cuba. He and his girlfriend were released by the hostage-taker, and they spoke to his father in New Brunswick, Canada, while waiting for another flight. "I didn't ask them too many questions; I was more concerned for their safety," the father said. "They were a bit shaken up. It was quite an experience." Another passenger, Brenda Grenier, called her husband and said the man apparently got aboard the plane as airport workers were loading bags. Grenier and her daughter were safe, her husband said by phone from his home in Nova Scotia, Canada. CNN's Joyce Joseph, Janet DiGiacomo, Jessica Jordan, Saeed Ahmed and Mike Brooks contributed to this report.

The incident involved **CanJet Flight 918**, a charter flight carrying mostly Canadian vacationers. The aircraft, a Boeing 737, had been scheduled to travel from **Halifax, Nova Scotia**, to **Santa Clara, Cuba**, with a stop in **Montego Bay, Jamaica**. There were roughly **180 people on board**, including passengers and crew, when the crisis began late Sunday night.

No passengers or crew members were killed or seriously injured.

## Gunman Boards Aircraft During Stopover

Authorities said the armed man breached airport security at Sangster International Airport and boarded the aircraft while it was on the ground. He was reportedly carrying a handgun and demanded to be flown off the island, with initial reports indicating he wanted the plane taken to **Cuba**.

Once aboard, the gunman robbed several passengers and created panic inside the cabin. Passengers described the scene as chaotic and terrifying, with many initially unsure whether the event was a robbery, a hijacking, or some other emergency.

Some passengers said they were ordered to keep their heads down and remain quiet. Others said they heard the man yelling demands and saw crew members attempting to calm the situation.

## Passengers Released, Crew Held Hostage

After negotiations began, the gunman released the passengers in stages. Women, children, and some elderly passengers were among those allowed off the aircraft early in the ordeal. Eventually, all passengers were released, but several crew members remained on board as hostages.

The CanJet crew were widely praised for their composure during the incident. Passengers later said the flight attendants and pilots remained calm and helped prevent the panic from escalating.

One passenger recalled that the crew “kept everyone as calm as possible” despite the uncertainty. Others said they feared they might never see their families again, and some sent text messages or made phone calls to relatives during the standoff.

## Jamaican Officials Respond

Jamaican police, military personnel, airport security, and government officials converged on the airport as the standoff unfolded. The aircraft was isolated on the tarmac, and the airport’s operations were disrupted while security forces established a perimeter.

Jamaican Prime Minister **Bruce Golding** was involved in monitoring the crisis, and senior Jamaican officials assisted in coordinating the response. Officials from Jamaica’s national security apparatus, police command, and airport authorities worked alongside negotiators to bring the situation to a peaceful conclusion.

The crisis drew international attention because the aircraft was Canadian-operated and the passengers were largely Canadian citizens. Canadian officials were also notified and monitored events closely.

## Negotiations Through the Night

Negotiators communicated with the gunman for several hours. Their priority was to secure the release of the remaining crew members without gunfire or injury.

Reports from Jamaican authorities indicated that the gunman appeared emotionally unstable and was making repeated demands. Negotiators worked to keep him engaged while tactical teams prepared for several possible outcomes.

The standoff lasted for hours into the early morning. Eventually, the gunman released the remaining crew members or was subdued after negotiations reached their final stage. Jamaican security forces then took him into custody.

Authorities later identified the suspect as **Stephen Fray**, a young Jamaican man. He was arrested and faced serious charges related to hijacking, robbery, illegal possession of a firearm, and kidnapping.

## Relief and Praise From Passengers

After being freed, passengers were taken to a secure area of the airport and later to hotels, where they were interviewed by police and assisted by airline and consular officials.

Many passengers reacted with relief, exhaustion, and disbelief. Some cried after leaving the aircraft. Others embraced family members or fellow travelers. Several passengers said they were grateful to be alive and praised both the crew and Jamaican authorities.

A number of passengers described the ordeal as “the longest night” of their lives. Some said they had believed the gunman might force the aircraft into the air; others feared he might start shooting if his demands were not met.

Despite the fear, passengers repeatedly credited the CanJet crew for remaining professional. The crew’s handling of the crisis was later recognized as a key factor in preventing injuries.

## Airport and Airline Response

Sangster International Airport temporarily suspended or restricted operations during the crisis. Flights were delayed while authorities dealt with the emergency and secured the area.

CanJet, a Canadian charter airline based in Halifax, said its primary concern was the safety and well-being of passengers and crew. The airline worked to arrange accommodations and onward travel for the passengers after the incident.

Canadian officials also expressed relief that the hostage situation ended without loss of life.

## Aftermath

The CanJet Flight 918 incident prompted scrutiny of airport security procedures in Jamaica, particularly how an armed man was able to breach security and board an international aircraft. Jamaican authorities promised a full investigation and review of airport security measures.

The peaceful resolution was credited to the restraint of the crew, the work of negotiators, and the coordinated response of Jamaican police, military, airport officials, and government leaders.

Although the incident ended without casualties, it left passengers and crew shaken and became one of the most serious aviation security scares in Jamaica’s recent history.
